claim: Proactive interference impairs access to a target memory when overlapping information has been stored prior to target learning.
source: A prominent case is proactive interference, where access to a target memory is impaired when overlapping information has been stored prior to target learning (Tulving and Watkins, 1974).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tulving and Watkins, 1974.

claim: Proactive interference impairment is typically ascribed to the conflict arising from the co-activation of competing memories.
source: This impairment is typically ascribed to the conflict arising from the co-activation of competing memories (Kliegl and Bäuml, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kliegl and Bäuml, 2021.

claim: Mid-frontal theta oscillations (3–8 Hz) have been identified as a reliable marker of cognitive conflict in general.
source: On a neurophysiological level, mid-frontal theta oscillations (3–8 Hz) have been identified as a reliable marker of cognitive conflict in general (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014) and mnemonic conflict specifically (Ferreira et al., 2014; Hanslmayr et al., 2010; Johansson et al., 2007; Staudigl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cavanagh and Frank, 2014 and other studies.

claim: Mid-frontal theta oscillations (3–8 Hz) have been identified as a reliable marker of mnemonic conflict specifically.
source: On a neurophysiological level, mid-frontal theta oscillations (3–8 Hz) have been identified as a reliable marker of cognitive conflict in general (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014) and mnemonic conflict specifically (Ferreira et al., 2014; Hanslmayr et al., 2010; Johansson et al., 2007; Staudigl et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferreira et al., 2014; Hanslmayr et al., 2010; Johansson et al., 2007; Staudigl et al., 2010.

claim: Increased theta amplitudes may facilitate the emergence of phase separation, where populations of neurons transmitting potentially interfering information are segregated in time along a theta cycle.
source: Increased theta amplitudes may facilitate the emergence of phase separation, where populations of neurons transmitting potentially interfering information are segregated in time along a theta cycle (Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004.

claim: Computational models assign a central role to the phase of the hippocampal theta oscillation in the ordered representation of multiplexed information.
source: On a theoretical level, computational models assign a central role to the phase of the hippocampal theta oscillation in the ordered representation of multiplexed information (Lakatos et al., 2005; Lisman, 2005; Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Nyhus and Curran, 2010; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple computational modeling studies.

claim: In rodents, bursts of gamma power reflecting sequences of spatial information processing are represented at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation.
source: Empirically, in rodents it has been shown that bursts of gamma power reflecting sequences of spatial information processing are represented at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation (Bragin et al., 1995; Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bragin et al., 1995 and Colgin et al., 2009.

claim: In humans, neural representations of items held in working memory or encoded into or retrieved from episodic memory cluster at distinct phases of the (hippocampal) theta rhythm.
source: Several recent studies in humans suggest that the neural representations of items held in working memory or encoded into or retrieved from episodic memory (Kerrén et al., 2018; Kunz et al., 2019; Pacheco Estefan et al., 2021) cluster at distinct phases of the (hippocampal) theta rhythm.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kerrén et al., 2018; Kunz et al., 2019; Pacheco Estefan et al., 2021.

claim: Low-frequency oscillations provide time windows for the selective processing and readout of distinct units of information.
source: These findings suggest that low-frequency oscillations provide time windows for the selective processing and readout of distinct units of information (Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lisman and Jensen, 2013.

claim: The oscillating interference resolution model leverages different phases of a theta oscillation to iteratively differentiate target from competitor memories.
source: One computational model leverages different phases of a theta oscillation to iteratively differentiate target from competitor memories (Norman et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Norman et al., 2006.

claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, a retrieval cue will activate associated units, representing target and competitor features, in a phase-dependent manner.
source: In this model, which we will henceforth refer to as the oscillating interference resolution model, a retrieval cue will activate associated units, representing target and competitor features, in a phase-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model from Norman et al., 2006.

claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, at medium levels of inhibition, the cue only activates the target units and no or few competitor features.
source: In the most desirable output state, at medium levels of inhibition, the cue only activates the target units and no or few competitor features.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, when inhibition is raised towards the peak of the oscillation, only strong features of the target memory will remain active.
source: When inhibition is raised towards the peak of the oscillation, only strong features of the target memory will remain active, and the model learns (via contrastive Hebbian learning) to strengthen through long-term potentiation (LTP) the weaker target nodes that did not survive the higher inhibition levels.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, the model learns to strengthen through long-term potentiation (LTP) the weaker target nodes that did not survive the higher inhibition levels.
source: When inhibition is raised towards the peak of the oscillation, only strong features of the target memory will remain active, and the model learns (via contrastive Hebbian learning) to strengthen through long-term potentiation (LTP) the weaker target nodes that did not survive the higher inhibition levels.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, during the transition from a medium to a lower inhibition state towards the trough of the oscillation, activation spreads to more weakly associated units, including some competitor features.
source: Conversely, during the transition from a medium to a lower inhibition state towards the trough of the oscillation, activation spreads to more weakly associated units, including some competitor features.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: In the oscillating interference resolution model, the opposite phase is used to identify and punish overly strong features of the competing memory through long-term depression (LTD).
source: This opposite phase is used to identify and punish overly strong features of the competing memory through long-term depression (LTD).
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: The oscillating interference resolution mechanism is repeated across several cycles of an oscillation, which changes the similarity structure of memories into a state in which they are less likely to interfere with each other.
source: The mechanism (see Figure 1) is repeated across several cycles of an oscillation, which changes the similarity structure of memories into a state in which they are less likely to interfere with each other.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model and references Figure 1.

claim: A previous study provided proof-of-principle evidence that the reactivation of a single visual memory is rhythmically modulated by the hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: A previous study (Kerrén et al., 2018) provided proof-of-principle evidence that the reactivation of a single visual memory is rhythmically modulated by the hippocampal theta rhythm.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kerrén et al., 2018.

claim: Target and competitor memories become active, and can thus be decoded, at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation.
source: Based on the oscillating interference resolution model (Norman et al., 2006) and related theta-gamma models (e.g., Lisman and Idiart, 1995), we expected that target and competitor memories become active, and can thus be decoded, at different phases of the hippocampal theta oscillation, with only target features active at higher inhibition phases, and competitors surfacing as inhibition ramps down to medium and low levels (see Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis derived from the oscillating interference resolution model and related models, and references Figure 1d.

claim: Across several repetitions of the theta cycle, weak features of target memories are strengthened while overly strong features of competing memories are punished to make them less interfering on future cycles.
source: The model also assumes that across several repetitions of the theta cycle, weak features of target memories are strengthened while overly strong features of competing memories are punished to make them less interfering on future cycles.
evidence: The claim is based on the assumptions of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: The effects of the oscillating interference resolution dynamics will become visible across several repetitions of competitive retrieval and lead to an increasing phase separation.
source: We hypothesised that the effects of these dynamics will become visible across several repetitions of competitive retrieval and lead to an increasing phase separation because over time target memories become more likely to activate in the high-inhibition phase whereas competing memories require increasingly lower levels of inhibition to activate.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis derived from the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: The strengthening of target and weakening of competing memories should be reflected in corresponding changes in their decodability.
source: Lastly, in line with previous literature (Wimber et al., 2015), the strengthening of target and weakening of competing memories should also be reflected in corresponding changes in their decodability.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Wimber et al., 2015.

claim: Memory performance was significantly reduced in the competitive (M = 53.18%, SD = 19.20%) compared to the single-exposure (M = 57.71%, SD = 13.98%) condition, t(23) = 1.80, p<0.05.
source: The main planned comparison of interest showed that memory performance was indeed significantly reduced in the competitive (M = 53.18%, SD = 19.20%) compared to the single-exposure (M = 57.71%, SD = 13.98%) condition, t(23) = 1.80, p<0.05 (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2a.

claim: Retrieving a memory is more difficult when a previously encoded, now irrelevant associate competes for recall, indicative of proactive interference.
source: This confirms the first behavioural hypothesis (OSF) that retrieving a memory is more difficult when a previously encoded, now irrelevant associate competes for recall, indicative of proactive interference.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing reduced memory performance in the competitive condition.

claim: A significant difference was obtained between NC1 and NC2 (M = 78.88%, SD = 10.06%), t(23) = –11.91, p<0.05, demonstrating that a second encoding exposure improved performance compared to a single exposure.
source: A second post-hoc test showed that a significant difference was also obtained between NC1 and NC2 (M = 78.88%, SD = 10.06%), t(23) = –11.91, p<0.05, demonstrating that, unsurprisingly, a second encoding exposure improved performance compared to a single exposure.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: On trials where participants made an error, they showed a significantly above-chance (i.e. above 50%) probability of selecting the subcategory of the competitor (on average, 88.72%, SD = 10.62%; t(23) = 10.48, p<0.05).
source: On trials where participants made an error (i.e. selected 'object' though the target was a scene and vice versa), they showed a significantly above-chance (i.e. above 50%) probability of selecting the subcategory of the competitor (on average, 88.72%, SD = 10.62%; t(23) = 10.48, p<0.05), suggesting that their errors were not random but biased towards the category of the previously learned but now irrelevant associate (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2b.

claim: Participants' errors were not random but biased towards the category of the previously learned but now irrelevant associate.
source: On trials where participants made an error (i.e. selected 'object' though the target was a scene and vice versa), they showed a significantly above-chance (i.e. above 50%) probability of selecting the subcategory of the competitor (on average, 88.72%, SD = 10.62%; t(23) = 10.48, p<0.05), suggesting that their errors were not random but biased towards the category of the previously learned but now irrelevant associate (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing above-chance selection of competitor subcategories.

claim: The proportion of intrusions did not change significantly across repetitions (first: 88.08%, SD = 12.04%; second: 89.23%, SD = 10.62%; third: 88.85%, SD = 14.72%, Z = –54, p=0.59).
source: The proportion of intrusions did not change significantly across repetitions (first: 88.08%, SD = 12.04%; second: 89.23%, SD = 10.62%; third: 88.85%, SD = 14.72%, Z = –54, p=0.59; Wilcoxon signed-rank test of linear slope against zero).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no decrease across repetitions in behavioural accuracy for CC target items (Z = –0.73, p=0.47).
source: Similarly, we did not find a decrease across repetitions in behavioural accuracy for CC target items (Z = –0.73, p=0.47; Wilcoxon signed-rank test of linear slope against zero; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Across participants, the average number of intrusions in the CC correlated negatively with memory performance in the non-competitive conditions, r = –0.37, p=0.037, p<0.05.
source: Across participants, the average number of intrusions in the CC correlated negatively with memory performance in the non-competitive conditions, r = –0.37, p=0.037, p<0.05 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), indicating that better memory performance was generally associated with fewer intrusion errors.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Better memory performance was generally associated with fewer intrusion errors.
source: Across participants, the average number of intrusions in the CC correlated negatively with memory performance in the non-competitive conditions, r = –0.37, p=0.037, p<0.05 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), indicating that better memory performance was generally associated with fewer intrusion errors.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the negative correlation between intrusions and memory performance.

claim: The average response time for subjective recollection was 2.11 s (SD = 0.15 s) when collapsing across all conditions and repetitions.
source: The average response time for subjective recollection (indicated by button press) was 2.11 s (SD = 0.15 s) when collapsing across all conditions and repetitions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Response times shortened across repetitions in all three conditions (CC: rep1: 2.29 s, rep2: 2.05 s, rep3: 2.04 s; Z = –2.89, p=0.004; NC1: rep1: 2.55 s, rep2: 2.37 s, rep3: 2.26 s; Z = 3.03, p=0.003; NC2: rep1: 2.01 s, rep2: 1.75 s, rep3: 1.68 s; Z = –4.17, p<0.001).
source: Response times shortened across repetitions in all three conditions (CC: rep1: 2.29 s, rep2: 2.05 s, rep3: 2.04 s; Z = –2.89, p=0.004; NC1: rep1: 2.55 s, rep2: 2.37 s, rep3: 2.26 s; Z = 3.03, p=0.003; NC2: rep1: 2.01 s, rep2: 1.75 s, rep3: 1.68 s; Z = –4.17, p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of linear slope against zero), suggesting that the time point when participants remembered the associate shifted and overall was faster after repeated recalls, as would be expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The time point when participants remembered the associate shifted and overall was faster after repeated recalls.
source: Response times shortened across repetitions in all three conditions (CC: rep1: 2.29 s, rep2: 2.05 s, rep3: 2.04 s; Z = –2.89, p=0.004; NC1: rep1: 2.55 s, rep2: 2.37 s, rep3: 2.26 s; Z = 3.03, p=0.003; NC2: rep1: 2.01 s, rep2: 1.75 s, rep3: 1.68 s; Z = –4.17, p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests of linear slope against zero), suggesting that the time point when participants remembered the associate shifted and overall was faster after repeated recalls, as would be expected.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing shortened response times across repetitions.

claim: A non-parametric cluster-based permutation test revealed a significant power increase when retrieving the target association in the CC compared to the NC2 condition (pcluster<0.05), ranging from approximately 500 to 700 ms post-cue.
source: A non-parametric cluster-based permutation test, focused on a time window of interest 0–1 s following cue onset and on the previously reported 3–8 Hz theta range, revealed a significant power increase when retrieving the target association in the CC compared to the NC2 condition (pcluster<0.05), ranging from approximately 500 to 700 ms post-cue (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2c.

claim: In addition to behavioural evidence for proactive interference, we also replicate previous work that established frontal theta power increases as a neural signature of competition.
source: In addition to behavioural evidence for proactive interference, we thus also replicate previous work that established frontal theta power increases as a neural signature of competition.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data showing theta power increases and citations to previous work.

claim: In terms of its topography, this frontal effect was more right-lateralised than the typically observed mid-frontal theta.
source: Note, however, that in terms of its topography, this frontal effect was more right-lateralised than the typically observed mid-frontal theta (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014), and might instead be more related to response conflict or response inhibition (for a review, see Aron et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and citations to Cavanagh and Frank, 2014 and Aron et al., 2004.

claim: This frontal effect might be more related to response conflict or response inhibition.
source: Note, however, that in terms of its topography, this frontal effect was more right-lateralised than the typically observed mid-frontal theta (Cavanagh and Frank, 2014), and might instead be more related to response conflict or response inhibition (for a review, see Aron et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the topography of the effect and a citation to Aron et al., 2004.

claim: Reliable (pcluster<0.05) above-chance decoding performance was found in a time window from 2.55 to 2.92 s post-cue onset.
source: This first decoding analysis indicated that reliable (pcluster<0.05) above-chance decoding performance was found in a time window from 2.55 to 2.92 s post-cue onset, somewhat later than the typical time window for reinstatement of associative memories in cued recall tests (for a review, see Staresina and Wimber, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The reliable above-chance decoding performance was somewhat later than the typical time window for reinstatement of associative memories in cued recall tests.
source: This first decoding analysis indicated that reliable (pcluster<0.05) above-chance decoding performance was found in a time window from 2.55 to 2.92 s post-cue onset, somewhat later than the typical time window for reinstatement of associative memories in cued recall tests (for a review, see Staresina and Wimber, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data and a citation to Staresina and Wimber, 2019.

claim: No significant cluster could be identified when correcting for multiple comparisons across time points in the CC, indicating that overall reinstatement was less robust in the condition where two associates competed for recall.
source: Figure 2e shows the average target decoding accuracy in the CC. Classification performance peaked in time windows similar to the non-competitive condition. However, no significant cluster could be identified when correcting for multiple comparisons across time points, indicating that overall reinstatement was less robust in the condition where two associates competed for recall, potentially because this competition was associated with less confident target retrieval.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2e.

claim: Overall reinstatement was less robust in the condition where two associates competed for recall, potentially because this competition was associated with less confident target retrieval.
source: Figure 2e shows the average target decoding accuracy in the CC. Classification performance peaked in time windows similar to the non-competitive condition. However, no significant cluster could be identified when correcting for multiple comparisons across time points, indicating that overall reinstatement was less robust in the condition where two associates competed for recall, potentially because this competition was associated with less confident target retrieval.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing less robust reinstatement in the CC.

claim: Realigning the decoding data to the subjective recollection button press revealed two clusters of significant target classification preceding the button press by approximately 200 ms.
source: We thus conducted an additional analysis (not pre-registered, added as part of peer review process) realigning the decoding data to the subjective recollection button press, and thus to the time point when participants indicated they had the associated image back in mind. This method revealed two clusters of significant target classification preceding the button press by approximately 200 ms (Figure 2f).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2f.

claim: Target classification on correct trials was significantly stronger than on incorrect trials.
source: The realigned analysis further revealed that target classification on correct trials was significantly stronger than on incorrect trials (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2g.

claim: The classifiers are able to pick up categorical reactivation also in the CC, and this reactivation varies with behavioural performance in a meaningful way.
source: These results reaffirm that the classifiers are able to pick up categorical reactivation also in the CC, and that this reactivation varies with behavioural performance in a meaningful way.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing significant target classification and its relationship to behavioural performance.

claim: The lack of significant decoding in the cue-locked analyses is due to timing differences in memory reinstatement between conditions, trials, and participants, which is rectified when locking to the time point of subjective recollection.
source: They also suggest that the lack of significant decoding in the cue-locked analyses is due to timing differences in memory reinstatement between conditions, trials, and participants, which is rectified when locking to the time point of subjective recollection.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the comparison of cue-locked and response-locked analyses.

claim: A contrast of the decoding timelines between the first and third repetition revealed a significant increase (pcluster<0.05, 1.79–2.11 s; third repetition compared to chance pcluster=0.07) in decodability of the target memory approximately 2 s after cue onset.
source: A contrast of the decoding timelines between the first and third repetition revealed a significant increase (pcluster<0.05, 1.79–2.11 s; third repetition compared to chance pcluster=0.07) in decodability of the target memory approximately 2 s after cue onset (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: No corresponding cluster emerged when comparing the entire timeline of competitor reactivation between the first and third recall.
source: No corresponding cluster emerged when comparing the entire timeline of competitor reactivation between the first and third recall (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: An additional analysis testing for competitor evidence on incorrect trials revealed more robust competitor activation.
source: An additional analysis testing for competitor evidence on incorrect trials, when competitors are more likely to interfere, revealed more robust competitor activation (see Figure 2—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claim: A significant repetition-by-associate interaction was found (F(1,20) = 5.187, p=0.034), with a significant increase of target reactivation from first to third recall (first: 49.43%, SD = 4.08%; third: 53.14%, SD = 6.43%; t(20) = –2.46, p=0.02), and a numerical but non-significant decrease of competitor reactivation (first: 52.05%, SD = 4.55%; third: 50.82%, SD = 5.54%; t(20) = 1.1, p=0.29).
source: Zooming in on the time window where targets and competitors were maximally decodable (1.77–1.93 s after cue onset, puncorr<0.05, see Figure 2—figure supplement 2e), a significant repetition-by-associate interaction was found (F(1,20) = 5.187, p=0.034), with a significant increase of target reactivation from first to third recall (first: 49.43%, SD = 4.08%; third: 53.14%, SD = 6.43%; t(20) = –2.46, p=0.02), and a numerical but non-significant decrease of competitor reactivation (first: 52.05%, SD = 4.55%; third: 50.82%, SD = 5.54%; t(20) = 1.1, p=0.29) (Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2h.

claim: We observed a strengthening of the relevant target memory and a numerical but non-significant weakening of the competing memory across repetitions in this select time window.
source: Thus, we observed a strengthening of the relevant target memory and a numerical but non-significant weakening of the competing memory across repetitions in this select time window.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the data showing changes in target and competitor reactivation across repetitions.

claim: A significant correlation (r = 0.446, p=0.04) was found such that stronger reactivation of competitor memories positively correlated with a higher level of initial intrusions.
source: Lastly, taking inspiration from previous work on competitor reactivation and its relationship to behavioural memory interference (Newman and Norman, 2010), we extracted the average decoding across repetitions for the competitor memories from 0 to 1 s after cue onset and correlated this reactivation with the probability of intrusions in the first repetition. This revealed a significant correlation (r = 0.446, p=0.04; Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), such that stronger reactivation of competitor memories positively correlated with a higher level of initial intrusions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Target memories can be decoded from MEG signals when no competition is present.
source: Together, the cue-locked decoding results provide evidence that target memories can be decoded from MEG signals when no competition is present, while under conditions of interference, target reactivation is less robust in early trials but gradually increases over repetitions.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the decoding results.

claim: Under conditions of interference, target reactivation is less robust in early trials but gradually increases over repetitions.
source: Together, the cue-locked decoding results provide evidence that target memories can be decoded from MEG signals when no competition is present, while under conditions of interference, target reactivation is less robust in early trials but gradually increases over repetitions.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the decoding results.

claim: This pattern could emerge due to the gradual strengthening of the relevant target memory or due to reduced interference from the competing memory.
source: This pattern could emerge due to the gradual strengthening of the relevant target memory or due to reduced interference from the competing memory.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering possible explanations for the observed pattern.

claim: When realigning the decoding to the subjective time of recollection, we found significant target decoding, indicating that temporal variance in memory reactivation could explain the non-significant results in the cue-locked analysis.
source: When instead realigning the decoding to the subjective time of recollection, we found significant target decoding, indicating that temporal variance in memory reactivation could explain the non-significant results in the cue-locked analysis.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the comparison of cue-locked and response-locked analyses.

claim: IRASA identified 3 Hz as the frequency with the highest power for both target and competitor memories.
source: The analysis identified 3 Hz as the frequency with the highest power for both target and competitor memories (same peak frequency was also observed for the first repetition; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b), and power at 3 Hz exceeded the 95th percentile of the empirical chance distribution generated from surrogate-label classifiers (Figure 3a and b, red line indicating significant deviation).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3a, b, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: Power at 3 Hz exceeded the 95th percentile of the empirical chance distribution generated from surrogate-label classifiers.
source: The analysis identified 3 Hz as the frequency with the highest power for both target and competitor memories (same peak frequency was also observed for the first repetition; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b), and power at 3 Hz exceeded the 95th percentile of the empirical chance distribution generated from surrogate-label classifiers (Figure 3a and b, red line indicating significant deviation).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3a and b.

claim: For the NC, the peak frequency was also in the low theta range but slightly faster (4–5 Hz).
source: For the NC, the peak frequency was also in the low theta range but slightly faster (4–5 Hz; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: Fidelity values for target and competitor memories were significantly modulated by the hippocampal theta rhythm at 3 Hz.
source: Results of the phase modulation analysis linking decoding fidelity to the phase of the hippocampal 3 Hz oscillation. Fidelity values for target (e) and competitor memories (f) were significantly modulated by the hippocampal theta rhythm at 3 Hz.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3e and f.

claim: The third retrieval repetition shows significant modulation exceeding the 95th percentile.
source: Distribution of each individual's modulation index (MI) with the 95th percentile subtracted. The third retrieval repetition shows significant modulation exceeding the 95th percentile (red line).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3d.

claim: At repetition 3, there was a phase shift of on average 34° that was statistically coherent across subjects and significantly different from zero, indicative of robust target–competitor phase segregation.
source: At repetition 3 (right circular plot), there was a phase shift of on average 34° that was statistically coherent across subjects and significantly different from zero, indicative of robust target–competitor phase segregation.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4a.

claim: We found a consistent phase difference between target and competitor reactivation exclusively in the last repetition (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, z(20) = 5.03, p=0.005), clustered around a mean angular difference of 34°.
source: We found a consistent phase difference between target and competitor reactivation exclusively in the last repetition (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, z(20) = 5.03, p=0.005), clustered around a mean angular difference of 34°.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A test against zero phase shift confirmed that this target–competitor distance was significantly different from zero difference (z(20) = 8.48, p=0.004).
source: Furthermore, a test against zero phase shift confirmed that this target–competitor distance was significantly different from zero difference (z(20) = 8.48, p=0.004).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: This was not the case for all repetitions averaged, (z(20) = 0.84, p=0.44), nor for the first (z(20) = 2.19, p=0.11) or second (z(20) = 1.76, p=0.17) repetition separately.
source: This was not the case for all repetitions averaged, (z(20) = 0.84, p=0.44), nor for the first (z(20) = 2.19, p=0.11) or second (z(20) = 1.76, p=0.17) repetition separately (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4a.

claim: There was no significant difference in target–competitor phase separation between the first and third repetition when comparing the difference in mean angle (z(20) = 1.09, p=0.29).
source: Furthermore, there was no significant difference in target–competitor phase separation between the first and third repetition when comparing the difference in mean angle (z(20) = 1.09, p=0.29).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Finding the separation between target and competitor memories only in the last repetition rather than throughout the entire recall phase deviates from our pre-registered hypothesis.
source: Finding the separation between target and competitor memories only in the last repetition rather than throughout the entire recall phase deviates from our pre-registered hypothesis, although paralleling the phase modulation results reported above.
evidence: The claim is an inference comparing the results to the pre-registered hypothesis.

claim: The phase distance analysis partly confirms our hypotheses, indicating that competing memories become increasingly separated along the hippocampal theta rhythm over time, with significant phase separation emerging after several recall cycles.
source: Overall, the phase distance analysis thus partly confirms our hypotheses, indicating that competing memories become increasingly separated along the hippocampal theta rhythm over time, with significant phase separation emerging after several recall cycles.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the phase distance analysis results.

claim: When splitting the phase difference in the third repetition by behavioural intrusion score, the high-intrusion group had a mean phase separation angle close to zero.
source: When splitting the phase difference in the third repetition by behavioural intrusion score, the high-intrusion group had a mean phase separation angle close to zero (top), while the low-intrusion group had a mean separation angle of 57° (bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 4b.

claim: The low-intrusion group had a mean separation angle of 57°.
source: When splitting the phase difference in the third repetition by behavioural intrusion score, the high-intrusion group had a mean phase separation angle close to zero (top), while the low-intrusion group had a mean separation angle of 57° (bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 4b.

claim: The high-intrusion group had a mean separation angle of 7° that was not significantly different from zero (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, z(9) = 1.77, p=0.17).
source: We found that the high-intrusion group had a mean separation angle of 7° that was not significantly different from zero (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, z(9) = 1.77, p=0.17).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The low-intrusion group showed a mean phase separation of 57° that significantly clustered around this angle (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, z(9) = 3.74, p=0.02).
source: The low-intrusion group, by contrast, showed a mean phase separation of 57° that significantly clustered around this angle (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, z(9) = 3.74, p=0.02); however, we found no significant deviation from zero phase shift in this subgroup of participants (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity with a specified mean angle of 0, z(9) = 3.32, p=0.069).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: We found no significant deviation from zero phase shift in the low-intrusion subgroup of participants (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity with a specified mean angle of 0, z(9) = 3.32, p=0.069).
source: The low-intrusion group, by contrast, showed a mean phase separation of 57° that significantly clustered around this angle (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity, z(9) = 3.74, p=0.02); however, we found no significant deviation from zero phase shift in this subgroup of participants (Rayleigh test for non-uniformity with a specified mean angle of 0, z(9) = 3.32, p=0.069).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: A statistical comparison of the phase separation angle in the high- and low-intrusion groups did not indicate a difference between the mean of the high- and low-intrusion groups' separation angle (Z = 43, p=0.85).
source: A statistical comparison of the phase separation angle in the high- and low-intrusion groups (Wilcoxon signed-rank test in non-circular space, see 'Materials and methods') did not indicate a difference between the mean of the high- and low-intrusion groups' separation angle (Z = 43, p=0.85).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: This analysis suggests that only low-intrusion participants exhibit significant phase separation by the end of the task, which can be taken as an indication that more neural differentiation of overlapping memories along the theta cycle relates to more successful behavioural differentiation.
source: In sum, this analysis suggests that only low-intrusion participants exhibit significant phase separation by the end of the task, which can be taken as an indication that more neural differentiation of overlapping memories along the theta cycle relates to more successful behavioural differentiation.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the analysis of phase separation in high- and low-intrusion groups.

claim: A cross-correlation revealed a significant cluster starting approximately 1 s after cue onset and lasting until the end of the trial, with a maximum lag of 30° phase angle.
source: The analysis revealed a significant cluster starting approximately 1 s after cue onset and lasting until the end of the trial, with a maximum lag of 30° phase angle (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4c.

claim: This finding suggests that the reactivation of competitor memories is lagging 30° behind the reactivation of target memories.
source: This finding suggests that the reactivation of competitor memories is lagging 30° behind the reactivation of target memories.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: Visual inspection suggests a temporal shift, and sometimes even phase opposition, between target and competitor decoding in most participants.
source: The second additional analysis used the average target and competitor fidelity timecourse of each participant, filtered at 3 Hz and shown individually in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a. Visual inspection already suggests a temporal shift, and sometimes even phase opposition, between target and competitor decoding in most participants.
evidence: The claim is based on visual inspection of the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The resulting phase separation suggests a continuous lag of approximately 45° between the two competing memories.
source: To formally quantify the phase shift on a group level, we subtracted in complex space, for each time bin, the phase angle of the target from the angle of the competitor. The resulting phase separation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b) is consistent with the cross-correlation results shown in Figure 4c and suggests a continuous lag of approximately 45° between the two competing memories.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The results of these two analyses on the continuous fidelity timecourses are consistent with the phase shift identified when looking at the classifier-peak-to-hippocampal-theta locking, and provide further evidence for a temporal segregation between target and competitor reactivations during the last retrieval repetition.
source: The results of these two analyses on the continuous fidelity timecourses are thus consistent with the phase shift identified when looking at the classifier-peak-to-hippocampal-theta locking, and provide further evidence for a temporal segregation between target and competitor reactivations during the last retrieval repetition.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the comparison of different analyses.

claim: The present results demonstrate that the neural signatures of two competing memories become increasingly phase separated over time along the theta rhythm.
source: In line with its predictions, the present results demonstrate that the neural signatures of two competing memories become increasingly phase separated over time along the theta rhythm.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Larger phase differences were associated with fewer intrusion errors from the interfering memories.
source: Furthermore, larger phase differences were associated with fewer intrusion errors from the interfering memories.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: These findings support the existence of a phase-coding mechanism along the cycle of a slow oscillation that adaptively separates competing mnemonic representations, minimising their temporal overlap.
source: These findings support the existence of a phase-coding mechanism along the cycle of a slow oscillation that adaptively separates competing mnemonic representations, minimising their temporal overlap (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Norman et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results and is supported by citations to Lisman and Idiart, 1995 and Norman et al., 2006.

claim: In the third and final recall repetition target and competitor memories showed a significant phase shift with an average distance of 34°.
source: Supporting our hypotheses, in the third and final recall repetition target and competitor memories showed a significant phase shift with an average distance of 34° (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4a and b.

claim: Larger phase separation angles in individual participants were related to lower levels of behavioural interference.
source: Larger phase separation angles in individual participants were related to lower levels of behavioural interference.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Participants with low levels of memory intrusions showed a significant phase difference of 57°, while high-intrusion participants showed a non-significant 7° phase shift on average.
source: Participants with low levels of memory intrusions showed a significant phase difference of 57°, while high-intrusion participants showed a non-significant 7° phase shift on average (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 4b.

claim: In the last repetition, a significant phase modulation was found for both target and competitor memories such that the fidelity of their neural reactivation was rhythmically modulated by the dominant 3 Hz rhythm.
source: Also in the last repetition, a significant phase modulation was found for both target and competitor memories such that the fidelity of their neural reactivation was rhythmically modulated by the dominant 3 Hz rhythm (Figure 3e and f).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references Figure 3e and f.

claim: A significant cluster of cross-correlation of the continuous target and competitor decoding timecourses suggested an average phase lag of 30°.
source: Finally, a significant cluster of cross-correlation of the continuous target and competitor decoding timecourses also suggested an average phase lag of 30°, complementing the analyses that explicitly relate classification performance to hippocampal theta phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: These results largely confirm our predictions derived from the oscillating interference resolution model, supporting a central role for slow oscillations in orchestrating memory recall by temporally segregating potentially interfering memories.
source: Though deviating from the pre-registered hypotheses in some respects as discussed below, these results largely confirm our predictions derived from the oscillating interference resolution model (Norman et al., 2006), supporting a central role for slow oscillations in orchestrating memory recall by temporally segregating potentially interfering memories.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results and is supported by a citation to Norman et al., 2006.

claim: Repeated recall is known to induce enhancement of the retrieved memories.
source: Though not tested behaviourally in this study, repeated recall is known to induce enhancement of the retrieved memories (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Rowland, 2014) and forgetting of non-retrieved, competing memories (Anderson et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karpicke and Roediger, 2008 and Rowland, 2014.

claim: Repeated recall is known to induce forgetting of non-retrieved, competing memories.
source: Though not tested behaviourally in this study, repeated recall is known to induce enhancement of the retrieved memories (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Rowland, 2014) and forgetting of non-retrieved, competing memories (Anderson et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 1994.

claim: Evidence for the up- and downregulation of neural target and competitor patterns, respectively, has previously been shown in fMRI studies.
source: Evidence for the up- and downregulation of neural target and competitor patterns, respectively, has previously been shown in fMRI studies (e.g. Kuhl et al., 2007; Wimber et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kuhl et al., 2007 and Wimber et al., 2015.

claim: We found neural evidence for both target strengthening and competitor weakening within the time window of maximum memory reactivation.
source: In this work, we found neural evidence for both target strengthening and competitor weakening within the time window of maximum memory reactivation (Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2h.

claim: The increase in target evidence was more robust than the decrease in competitor evidence, with the latter not surviving multiple comparisons correction across the entire recall time window.
source: The increase in target evidence was more robust than the decrease in competitor evidence, with the latter not surviving multiple comparisons correction across the entire recall time window.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: When analysing only incorrect trials, we found moderate evidence for the neural reactivation of competitor memories.
source: When instead analysing only incorrect trials, we found moderate evidence for the neural reactivation of competitor memories (Figure 2—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 2d.

claim: The relatively stable levels of competitor reactivation over repetitions might be due to the lack of feedback in our task, allowing little adjustment of incorrect responses.
source: The relatively stable levels of competitor reactivation over repetitions might also be due to the lack of feedback in our task, allowing little adjustment of incorrect responses, as also reflected in the flat behavioural intrusion index (Figure 2b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering a possible explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: Our results suggest that dynamic changes in overlapping memories can be tracked using MEG.
source: Overall, however, and in line with recent EEG work (Bramão et al., 2022), our results suggest that dynamic changes in overlapping memories can be tracked using MEG.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results and is supported by a citation to Bramão et al., 2022.

claim: Decoding of target and competitor memories in the high-interference (CC) condition was generally less robust than decoding of target memories in the low-interference (NC) conditions.
source: Decoding of target and competitor memories in the high-interference (CC) condition was generally less robust than decoding of target memories in the low-interference (NC) conditions.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: One challenge for time-resolved decoding of reactivated memory content is the considerable variance in the timing of memory recall across trials, conditions, and participants, likely affecting the timing in neural pattern reinstatement.
source: Generally, one challenge for time-resolved decoding of reactivated memory content is the considerable variance in the timing of memory recall across trials, conditions, and participants, likely affecting the timing in neural pattern reinstatement.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental results and general knowledge about decoding methods.

claim: Previous work suggests that the phase of theta oscillations is reset by a memory cue and remains relatively stationary for a period of time.
source: Most importantly, previous work suggests that the phase of theta oscillations is reset by a memory cue and remains relatively stationary for a period of time (see Rizzuto et al., 2006; Ter Wal et al., 2021), such that the locking of memory reactivations to the theta rhythm should be most coherent when aligned to cue onset.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rizzuto et al., 2006 and Ter Wal et al., 2021.

claim: The locking of memory reactivations to the theta rhythm should be most coherent when aligned to cue onset.
source: Most importantly, previous work suggests that the phase of theta oscillations is reset by a memory cue and remains relatively stationary for a period of time (see Rizzuto et al., 2006; Ter Wal et al., 2021), such that the locking of memory reactivations to the theta rhythm should be most coherent when aligned to cue onset.
evidence: The claim is an inference from previous work cited.

claim: The functional relevance of slow oscillations in regulating the excitation–inhibition balance of specific neural assemblies has featured strongly in other computational models.
source: The functional relevance of slow oscillations in regulating the excitation–inhibition balance of specific neural assemblies has featured strongly in other computational models too, and these models are supported by our findings at various levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by general knowledge of computational models.

claim: The theta-gamma model assumes that the coupling of gamma bursts to specific theta phases provides a timing mechanism for ordering sequences of items in working memory.
source: Most relevant in the present context is the theta-gamma model (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Lisman and Jensen, 2013), which assumes that the coupling of gamma bursts to specific theta phases provides a timing mechanism for ordering sequences of items in working memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lisman and Idiart, 1995 and Lisman and Jensen, 2013.

claim: In the theta-gamma model, a gamma burst reflects the firing of a local cell assembly representing a distinct unit of information.
source: Here, a gamma burst reflects the firing of a local cell assembly representing a distinct unit of information, while the phase of the slower theta oscillation rhythmically modulates the excitability of these local neural assemblies, and feedback inhibition allows for an organised, non-overlapping firing sequence across the theta cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the theta-gamma model.

claim: In the theta-gamma model, the phase of the slower theta oscillation rhythmically modulates the excitability of local neural assemblies.
source: Here, a gamma burst reflects the firing of a local cell assembly representing a distinct unit of information, while the phase of the slower theta oscillation rhythmically modulates the excitability of these local neural assemblies, and feedback inhibition allows for an organised, non-overlapping firing sequence across the theta cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the theta-gamma model.

claim: In the theta-gamma model, feedback inhibition allows for an organised, non-overlapping firing sequence across the theta cycle.
source: Here, a gamma burst reflects the firing of a local cell assembly representing a distinct unit of information, while the phase of the slower theta oscillation rhythmically modulates the excitability of these local neural assemblies, and feedback inhibition allows for an organised, non-overlapping firing sequence across the theta cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the theta-gamma model.

claim: In humans, studies using episodic and working memory tasks have provided evidence for a theta-gamma code.
source: In humans, studies using episodic and working memory tasks have provided evidence for such a theta-gamma code (Bahramisharif et al., 2018; Canolty et al., 2006; Fuentemilla et al., 2010; Griffiths et al., 2021; Herweg et al., 2020; Heusser et al., 2016; Karlsson et al., 2022; Reddy et al., 2021; Ten Oever et al., 2020; Ter Wal et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The oscillating interference resolution model and theta-gamma phase-coding models share the fundamental assumption that slow oscillations regulate the excitation–inhibition balance of local neural assemblies.
source: The oscillating interference resolution model (Norman et al., 2006) and theta-gamma phase-coding models share the fundamental assumption that slow oscillations regulate the excitation–inhibition balance of local neural assemblies (Buzsáki, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Norman et al., 2006 and Buzsáki, 2006.

claim: Theta-gamma code models were developed to explain how the brain can handle ongoing states of high attentional or working memory load, where multiple distinct items need to be kept separated and organised.
source: Theta-gamma code models were developed to explain how the brain can handle ongoing states of high attentional or working memory load, where multiple distinct items need to be kept separated and organised.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of theta-gamma code models.

claim: The oscillating interference resolution model is a learning model and thus explicitly oriented towards optimising future network states.
source: The oscillating interference resolution model (Norman et al., 2006) is a learning model and thus explicitly oriented towards optimising future network states.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model from Norman et al., 2006.

claim: The oscillating interference resolution model employs fluctuating inhibition to actively shape memory representations, with the goal to minimise future overlap and interference.
source: It employs fluctuating inhibition to actively shape memory representations, with the goal to minimise future overlap and interference.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: One intracranial study using a virtual navigation paradigm showed that the neural representations of potentially interfering spatial goal locations are coupled to distinct phases of the hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: However, one intracranial study using a virtual navigation paradigm showed that the neural representations of potentially interfering spatial goal locations are coupled to distinct phases of the hippocampal theta rhythm (Kunz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kunz et al., 2019.

claim: Phase precession and theta coupling of neuronal firing during goal-directed navigation have been shown in human hippocampal single-unit recordings.
source: Phase precession and theta coupling of neuronal firing during goal-directed navigation have also been shown in human hippocampal single-unit recordings (Qasim et al., 2021; Watrous et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Qasim et al., 2021 and Watrous et al., 2018.

claim: The present results directly support the idea that phase coding can temporally separate co-active, competing memory representations in the human brain.
source: The present results directly support the idea that phase coding can temporally separate co-active, competing memory representations in the human brain.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The results suggest that such a code adaptively evolves across repeated target retrievals, in line with the idea that oscillating excitation–inhibition can optimise learning with respect to future access to the relevant target memory.
source: They additionally suggest that such a code adaptively evolves across repeated target retrievals, in line with the idea that oscillating excitation–inhibition can optimise learning with respect to future access to the relevant target memory.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: A second prominent computational model focuses on different functional operations within the hippocampal circuit at opposing phases of the theta rhythm, with one half of the hippocampal theta cycle devoted to the encoding of new incoming information, and the other half to the recovery of internally stored information.
source: A second prominent computational model focuses on different functional operations within the hippocampal circuit at opposing phases of the theta rhythm, with one half of the hippocampal theta cycle devoted to the encoding of new incoming information, and the other half to the recovery of internally stored information (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Kunec et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hasselmo et al., 2002 and Kunec et al., 2005.

claim: In humans, previous EEG work and a recent study investigating rhythmic modulations of reaction times have provided evidence for process separation along the theta cycle.
source: In humans, previous EEG work Kerrén et al., 2018 and a recent study investigating rhythmic modulations of reaction times Ter Wal et al., 2021 have provided evidence for such process separation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kerrén et al., 2018 and Ter Wal et al., 2021.

claim: Target and competitor reactivations peaked at distinct theta phases, with an average separation angle of approximately 35°, and 57° in the low-intrusion group that presumably reached optimal interference resolution.
source: In the present study, target and competitor reactivations peaked at distinct theta phases, with an average separation angle of approximately 35°, and 57° in the low-intrusion group that presumably reached optimal interference resolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: This observation is consistent with a framework where both targets and competitors are reactivated during the retrieval portion of a theta cycle, but with sufficient phase separation to allow for differentiation in time.
source: This observation is consistent with a framework where both targets and competitors are reactivated during the retrieval portion of a theta cycle (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Kunec et al., 2005), but with sufficient phase separation to allow for differentiation in time.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results and is supported by citations to Hasselmo et al., 2002 and Kunec et al., 2005.

claim: The oscillating interference resolution model dedicates the entire theta cycle to retrieval operations and would thus predict temporal distances of up to 180° between targets and competitors.
source: Note, however, that the oscillating interference resolution model (Norman et al., 2006) dedicates the entire theta cycle to retrieval operations (as depicted in Figure 1d) and would thus predict temporal distances of up to 180° between targets and competitors.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model and references Figure 1d.

claim: The two models may not necessarily be incompatible, especially when considering that encoding and retrieval computations take place in different subcircuits of the hippocampus.
source: The two models may not necessarily be incompatible, especially when considering that encoding and retrieval computations take place in different subcircuits of the hippocampus (Hasselmo et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is speculative and is supported by a citation to Hasselmo et al., 2002.

claim: One prediction of the oscillating interference resolution model is the non-monotonic plasticity hypothesis, derived from the learning dynamics along the oscillatory cycle.
source: Other predictions of the oscillating interference resolution model (Norman et al., 2006) relate to the neural overlap in spatial patterns and have been tested primarily in fMRI studies. One such prediction is the non-monotonic plasticity hypothesis, derived from the same learning dynamics along the oscillatory cycle as described above.
evidence: The claim is based on the description of the oscillating interference resolution model from Norman et al., 2006.

claim: If a competitor is sufficiently strong to be co-activated in the high-inhibition (target) phase, it will benefit from synaptic strengthening of common connections and thus be integrated with the target memory.
source: If a competitor is sufficiently strong to be co-activated in the high-inhibition (target) phase, it will benefit from synaptic strengthening of common connections and thus be integrated with the target memory.
evidence: The claim is based on the non-monotonic plasticity hypothesis from the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: Moderately co-active competitors will be subject to synaptic depression and as a result become differentiated from the target memory.
source: Moderately co-active competitors, on the other hand, will be subject to synaptic depression and as a result become differentiated from the target memory (Ritvo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on the non-monotonic plasticity hypothesis and is supported by a citation to Ritvo et al., 2019.

claim: Evidence for non-monotonic plasticity comes from fMRI work that directly tracks changes in the similarity of target and competitor representations in terms of their spatial patterns.
source: Evidence for non-monotonic plasticity comes from fMRI work that directly tracks changes in the similarity of target and competitor representations in terms of their spatial patterns (Hulbert and Norman, 2015; Wammes et al., 2022), and the representational changes dependent on the level of (co)activation of overlapping memories (Detre et al., 2013; Lewis-Peacock and Norman, 2014; Poppenk and Norman, 2014; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple fMRI studies.

claim: fMRI studies investigating representational change resulting from repeated learning or recall have found evidence for differentiation or integration of overlapping memories in hippocampus, late sensory cortex, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Indirectly related, fMRI studies investigating representational change resulting from repeated learning or recall have also found evidence for differentiation or integration of overlapping memories in hippocampus, late sensory cortex, and prefrontal cortex (Favila et al., 2016; Hulbert and Norman, 2015; Kim et al., 2017; Kuhl et al., 2010; Schlichting and Preston, 2015; Wimber et al., 2015), and sometimes observed both in the same study but in different regions (Molitor et al., 2021; Schlichting and Preston, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple fMRI studies.

claim: There is a straightforward agreement between spatial and temporal separation in this network model.
source: Arguably, however, there is a straightforward agreement between spatial and temporal separation in this network model.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering an interpretation of the relationship between spatial and temporal separation.

claim: Strong competitors would tend to co-activate in the high-inhibition phase and thus be co-strengthened and integrated via LTP.
source: Strong competitors would tend to co-activate in the high-inhibition phase and thus be co-strengthened and integrated via LTP (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Hebb, 1949), whereas moderately co-active competitor memories would tend to co-activate only at lower levels of inhibition, which according to the model would lead to LTD.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the oscillating interference resolution model and is supported by citations to Bliss and Lomo, 1973 and Hebb, 1949.

claim: Moderately co-active competitor memories would tend to co-activate only at lower levels of inhibition, which according to the model would lead to LTD.
source: Strong competitors would tend to co-activate in the high-inhibition phase and thus be co-strengthened and integrated via LTP (Bliss and Lomo, 1973; Hebb, 1949), whereas moderately co-active competitor memories would tend to co-activate only at lower levels of inhibition, which according to the model would lead to LTD.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the oscillating interference resolution model.

claim: Our data support the idea that low temporal separation is related to integration, behaviourally.
source: Our data support the idea that low temporal separation is related to integration, behaviourally.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The high-intrusion group had a mean phase difference of 7° between target and competitor memories, theoretically in line with a time window of strong co-firing hence synaptic strengthening.
source: The high-intrusion group had a mean phase difference of 7° between target and competitor memories, theoretically in line with a time window of strong co-firing hence synaptic strengthening.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Integration might have led to higher amounts of intrusions.
source: Integration might thus have led to higher amounts of intrusions (Brunec et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is speculative and is supported by a citation to Brunec et al., 2020.

claim: In the low-intrusion group, more pronounced phase separation between target and competitor memories (57° on average) might have led to only moderate co-firing and hence promoted differentiation, resulting in lower levels of behavioural interference.
source: In the low-intrusion group, more pronounced phase separation between target and competitor memories (57° on average) might have led to only moderate co-firing and hence promoted differentiation, resulting in lower levels of behavioural interference.
evidence: The claim is speculative, offering an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Temporal separation could be a prerequisite for spatial differentiation.
source: Although speculative, temporal separation could be a prerequisite for spatial differentiation.
evidence: The claim is speculative.

claim: Previous studies have indicated large variations in the peak theta frequency in humans.
source: A priori we included the entire theta band in our pre-registration as previous studies have indicated large variations in the peak theta frequency in humans (Goyal et al., 2020; Jacobs, 2014; Kerrén et al., 2018; Lega et al., 2016; Ter Wal et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In a previous study, reactivations of target memories were most consistently coupled to a hippocampal 7–8 Hz oscillation, even though a slower 3–4 Hz peak was also present.
source: For example, in our previous study we found that reactivations of target memories were most consistently coupled to a hippocampal 7–8 Hz oscillation, even though a slower 3–4 Hz peak was also present (Kerrén et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kerrén et al., 2018.

claim: Slower 2–3 Hz oscillations dominated behaviour and hippocampal signals specifically when responses depended on memory.
source: In another study, Ter Wal et al., 2021 found that slower 2–3 Hz oscillations dominated behaviour and hippocampal signals specifically when responses depended on memory, consistent with other intracranial work reporting pronounced slow theta oscillations in the human hippocampus during memory tasks (Goyal et al., 2020; Lega et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ter Wal et al., 2021, Goyal et al., 2020, and Lega et al., 2012.

claim: In working memory, it has been demonstrated that theta oscillations slow down with increasing memory load.
source: In working memory, it has even been demonstrated that theta oscillations slow down with increasing memory load (Fell et al., 2011; Wolinski et al., 2018), in line with the theoretical idea that slower rhythms accommodate better phase separation (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fell et al., 2011 and Wolinski et al., 2018.

claim: Slower rhythms accommodate better phase separation.
source: In working memory, it has even been demonstrated that theta oscillations slow down with increasing memory load (Fell et al., 2011; Wolinski et al., 2018), in line with the theoretical idea that slower rhythms accommodate better phase separation (Lisman and Idiart, 1995; Lisman and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lisman and Idiart, 1995 and Lisman and Jensen, 2013.

claim: Conditions in which only one associate needs to be remembered showed slightly faster rhythmic peaks (4–5 Hz) than the condition in which two associates compete for retrieval (3–4 Hz).
source: Descriptively, such theta slowing was evident in the present data when comparing the frequency profiles of rhythmic memory reactivation between NC and CC conditions, where conditions in which only one associate needs to be remembered showed slightly faster rhythmic peaks (4–5 Hz) than the condition in which two associates compete for retrieval (3–4 Hz, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phase coding offers an elegant theoretical solution to temporally segregate the processing of potentially interfering information.
source: Phase coding offers an elegant theoretical solution to temporally segregate the processing of potentially interfering information.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of phase coding.

claim: Much empirical evidence for phase sequencing along the hippocampal theta oscillation comes from spatial navigation work, both in rodents and humans.
source: Much empirical evidence for phase sequencing along the hippocampal theta oscillation comes from spatial navigation work, both in rodents and humans (Herweg et al., 2020; Kunz et al., 2019; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993; Reddy et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: We demonstrated that phase coding facilitates the separation of overlapping, associatively linked memories.
source: We here demonstrated that phase coding facilitates the separation of overlapping, associatively linked memories.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Together with the computational model used to derive these predictions, these findings offer a possible mechanism utilised by the human brain to resolve competition between simultaneously active memories.
source: Together with the computational model used to derive these predictions, these findings offer a possible mechanism utilised by the human brain to resolve competition between simultaneously active memories.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results and the computational model.

claim: These findings add to a growing literature showing that slow oscillations orchestrate the intricate timing of neural processing with direct, observable effects on behaviour.
source: More generally, they add to a growing literature showing that slow oscillations orchestrate the intricate timing of neural processing with direct, observable effects on behaviour.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the experimental results and general knowledge of the literature.
